sentences.text: This animal is recognized by its elongated, narrow snout and nasal bones that form a rigid structure separate from the nostril opening.
Although its skull shape mimicked that of plesiosaurs, the internal mouth structure resembled a primitive nothosaur, equipped with many sharp teeth designed for catching fish.
The creature reached a length of roughly three meters and possessed a stiff spine, indicating it moved by swinging its limbs instead of undulating its body.
Its overall body plan was similar to the aquatic Triassic reptiles known as notosaurs.
Scientists have identified seven distinct fossil occurrences of this genus.
The genus was formally described by Karl von Zittel in the year 1887.
A specific specimen examined by paleontologist Sues in 1987 served as the basis for the modern description of the animal.
While related nothosaur remains are widespread across Europe, skulls of this genus were found only within the Germanic Basin in the Upper Muschelkalk formation.
The initial discovery of the first skulls was made by H. V. Meyer.
Geissler was the first to describe the full skeletons, followed later by Strunz who proposed a new hypothesis regarding the animal.
Its vertebral column was stiff, similar to that of plesiosaurs, suggesting the use of paddle-like flippers for movement through water.
Studies of muscle grooves indicate the animal may have engaged in a slight form of subaquatic flying, with most propulsion generated by its hind limbs.
Specialized bone processes helped increase body density to counteract buoyancy, supporting an aquatic or semi-aquatic lifestyle.
Analysis of the humerus revealed that the inner region was filled with calcified cartilage incorporated into the endochondral bone.
The largest known humerus measures 245 millimeters in length and 45 millimeters in width at the mid-shaft.
The femur was longer than the humerus.
Histological study of the species Pistosaurus longaevus confirmed that the medullary region of the humerus contained calcified cartilage within the endochondral bone.
Paleontologist Diedrich concluded that a slight form of underwater flight began with this animal, based on the examination of the pectoral and pelvic girdles and muscle grooves.
Most of the propulsion was generated by the hind limbs.
Evidence of avascular necrosis in the forelimbs suggests the animal lived in aquatic or semi-aquatic environments.
It is proposed that the creature inhabited cold, open marine waters, surviving thanks to an effective metabolism.
The rigid spine implied the use of oar-like flippers for propulsion in the water.
A thickened crest crossed the front part of the coracoid, a trait shared with plesiosaurs.
Researchers believe this thickened coracoid crest was related to the compressive force generated by limb movement.
The genus was originally named by Meyer in 1839.
Meyer also named the genus Pistosaurus in that same year.
The genus includes the species Pistosaurus longaevus and possibly Pistosaurus grandaevus.
Both Pistosaurus and Plesiosauria belong to the Triassic-originating clade Pistosauroidea.
Initially, plesiosaurs were suggested to be related to Pistosauroidea, a group belonging to Triassic Eusauropterygia.
A discovery by Sander indicates that Augustasaurus is closely related to Pistosaurus, despite differences in the axial skeleton.
Fossils have been found in France and Germany and date to the Middle Triassic.
The animal lived during the Middle Triassic, approximately 240 million years ago, in what is now France and Germany.
It is unlikely Pistosaurus was a direct ancestor of plesiosaurs, though its mixed features suggest a close relationship.
It is debated whether Pistosauroidea were direct ancestors of plesiosaurs, as a new Augustasaurus specimen challenges this theory.
Based on new evidence, Pistosauroidea was reclassified as a paraphyletic group relative to Plesiosauria rather than their stem ancestors.
